independent_solution: Fall: v = g t, so K = (1/2) m g^2 t^2 rises as t^2 (curving upward) to its value at impact.

Contact: force proportional to compression makes the ball decelerate smoothly (spring-like) to rest at maximum compression (K = 0) and re-accelerate; the ball returns to its original height, so K after contact equals K before.

Rise: K = (1/2) m (v0 - g t')^2 falls to zero at the top, the mirror image of the fall. The rendered options (pinned page 1) show this shape (smooth dip to zero between two symmetric parabolic arcs) only in (B).

Normal to the plane is at theta to the vertical; incoming vertical velocity v0 has v0 cos(theta) into the plane and v0 sin(theta) down the slope. Elastic rebound reverses only the normal part, so the rebound speed is v0 at 2 theta to the vertical.
Across the plane: u = v0 cos(theta), a = -g cos(theta) -> back on the plane after T = 2 v0/g.
Along (downhill): d = v0 sin(theta) T + (1/2) g sin(theta) T^2 = 4 v0^2 sin(theta)/g.
questions.official_answer: A v0^2 sin(theta)/g as printed on pinned answers page 11 (the coefficient is printed as the letter 'A')

independent_solution: The wall reverses the molecule's normal velocity component (200 cos30 m/s), so the molecule's own momentum changes by 2 m (200 cos30) along the normal; the wall receives the equal and opposite impulse, so the momentum of the molecule + wall system is conserved.
The molecule rebounds with the same speed (the massive wall takes negligible kinetic energy), so kinetic energy is conserved: the collision is elastic.
questions.independent_answer: Yes, for the molecule + wall system (not the molecule alone); elastic
questions.official_answer: Yes, momentum of the molecule + wall system is conserved; since kinetic energy is also conserved, the collision is elastic
